analysis.body:
The Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey recorded 21.2% of utilities firms using AI in the latest period, up from 12.6% previously, making it one of the more measurable adoption jumps across surveyed sectors. That figure covers utilities under NAICS 22, while oil and gas extraction reports separately under mining, so the headline understates the breadth of AI deployment across energy as a whole.

The applications cluster in several distinct areas. On the grid side, the Department of Energy's Grid Modernization Initiative funds AI projects in real-time grid balancing, reactor optimization, and carbon capture, working through a Grid Modernization Laboratory Consortium that partners DOE national laboratories with the seven US Independent System Operators and Regional Transmission Organizations. The Electric Power Research Institute runs the utility sector's shared research layer, covering AI for grid resilience, wildfire-risk prediction, and asset-health monitoring. IEEE PES, the technical standards body, publishes the underlying standards for machine learning in power systems, grid cyber-defense, and distributed energy resource management. NextEra Energy, described as the largest US renewable producer, uses AI to forecast wind and solar yield, optimize battery dispatch, and automate plant maintenance across its fleet.

In upstream oil and gas, Baker Hughes embeds AI and automation across its oilfield technology portfolio, describing digitalization and artificial intelligence as enabling remote operations, risk reduction, and decarbonization. Geoteric applies deep learning directly to 3D seismic data, with its AI Hub letting geoscientists compare networks and parameters to map subsurface faults for exploration and production workflows; a customer quoted on its site describes the technology as revolutionizing upstream exploration and helping to digitize and decarbonize operations globally. On the forecasting side, Amperon sells AI-driven demand forecasts to utilities, traders, and asset operators, claiming its models can achieve up to 3x more accuracy than existing load forecasting solutions by ingesting 40,000 weather points from four vendors and analyzing about 25 weather variables every hour through an ensemble approach.

Vendors arrive through two routes: as equipment and as software. Siemens Energy ships AI controllers and digital-twin software for gas, wind, and grid assets, so for many operators the AI is embedded in hardware they are already buying rather than a separate procurement. Specialist pure-plays like Amperon occupy a distinct layer, selling accuracy improvements to trading desks and utility operations teams that need forecasting granularity the larger equipment vendors do not provide.

Energy occupies an unusual dual position in the AI economy: it is simultaneously a deployer of AI and the binding physical constraint on AI's growth. Per the Department of Energy, data centers consumed about 4.4% of US electricity in 2023 and are projected to reach between 6.7 and 12% by 2028, with AI identified as the primary driver. DOE has responded with the Speed to Power Initiative to accelerate large-scale grid infrastructure development and has announced plans to partner with private-sector developers to site AI data centers on DOE lands. The department also acknowledges the risk side directly, noting that AI systems may generate incorrect, unverifiable, and potentially harmful outputs, and that any use must properly understand and mitigate those risks, a posture that aligns with the sector's existing culture of operational safety and regulatory oversight.

For a decision-maker weighing deployment, the sourced evidence points to forecasting and predictive maintenance as the areas with the clearest near-term ROI claims, while grid-scale applications remain substantially federally funded and standards-dependent. The dual role of energy as AI's largest infrastructure constraint also means that power availability, not just software readiness, is a practical ceiling on how fast even willing operators can scale compute-intensive AI workloads internally.
